Regression Analysis for Boston

Nao Mimoto – Class Web Page

1. Preliminary

The dataset “Boston” comes with package MASS. When you load the package, it automatically loads the dataset as well.

library(MASS)   # install.packages("MASS")
Boston          # see the data
head(Boston)    # another way to see the data

?Boston         # see explanation for variables

  # 1  crim     per capita crime rate by town.
  # 2  zn       proportion of residential land zoned for lots over 25,000 sq.ft.
  # 3  indus    proportion of non-retail business acres per town.
  # 4  chas     Charles River dummy variable (= 1 if tract bounds river; 0 otherwise).
  # 5  nox      nitrogen oxides concentration (parts per 10 million).
  # 6  rm       average number of rooms per dwelling.
  # 7  age      proportion of owner-occupied units built prior to 1940.
  # 8  dis      weighted mean of distances to five Boston employment centres.
  # 9  rad      index of accessibility to radial highways.
  # 10 tax      full-value property-tax rate per $10,000.
  # 11 ptratio  pupil-teacher ratio by town.
  # 12 black    1000(Bk - 0.63)^2 where Bk is the proportion of blacks by town.
  # 13 lstat    lower status of the population (percent).
  # 14 medv     median value of owner-occupied homes in \$1000s.

  # 13 lstat = lower status of the population (percent)
  #      Proportion of population that is lower status
  #      = 1/2 (proportion of adults without,
  #      some high school education and proportion of male
  #      workers classified as laborers). The logarithmic
  #      specification implies that socioeconomic status
  #      distinctions mean more in the upper brackets of
  #      society than in the lower classes. Source: 1970 U. S. Census


2. Turn Boston into a tibble

Boston comes as data.frame. It is a good habit to turn all the data you work with into a tibble for consistency and conveinience. A tibble is a modern version of data.frame that can be worked on using pakages in tidyverse.

class(Boston)                 # show the class of Boston

# - it's data.frame not tibble
# it's better to turn it into tibble

library(tidyverse)            # install.packages("tidyverse")
Boston <- as_tibble(Boston)
Boston

class(Boston)             # now it should be a tibble
is_tibble(Boston)         # is Boston tibble now?
is.data.frame(Boston)     # it's still data.frame too

Boston                    # only first 10 rows will print by default

# print(Boston, n=100)    # if you want to see more rows
# view(Boston)            # spreadsheet-like view NOT RECOMMENDED
                          # CLOSE TO MOVE FORWARD


3. Set Response variable

I like to name response variable ‘resp’ so that I don’t have to adjust the code every time. It also makes clear what is Y (resp), and what is X (everything else).

library(tidyverse)

### set medv as the response variable
# Rename "medv" column as "resp" to streamline analysis.
Boston2 <- Boston %>% rename(resp=medv)
Boston2

4. Full Model: Regression with all variables

Reg01 <- lm(resp ~ . , data=Boston2)
summary(Reg01)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = resp ~ ., data = Boston2)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -15.595  -2.730  -0.518   1.777  26.199 
## 
## Coefficients:
##               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  3.646e+01  5.103e+00   7.144 3.28e-12 ***
## crim        -1.080e-01  3.286e-02  -3.287 0.001087 ** 
## zn           4.642e-02  1.373e-02   3.382 0.000778 ***
## indus        2.056e-02  6.150e-02   0.334 0.738288    
## chas         2.687e+00  8.616e-01   3.118 0.001925 ** 
## nox         -1.777e+01  3.820e+00  -4.651 4.25e-06 ***
## rm           3.810e+00  4.179e-01   9.116  < 2e-16 ***
## age          6.922e-04  1.321e-02   0.052 0.958229    
## dis         -1.476e+00  1.995e-01  -7.398 6.01e-13 ***
## rad          3.060e-01  6.635e-02   4.613 5.07e-06 ***
## tax         -1.233e-02  3.760e-03  -3.280 0.001112 ** 
## ptratio     -9.527e-01  1.308e-01  -7.283 1.31e-12 ***
## black        9.312e-03  2.686e-03   3.467 0.000573 ***
## lstat       -5.248e-01  5.072e-02 -10.347  < 2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 4.745 on 492 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.7406, Adjusted R-squared:  0.7338 
## F-statistic: 108.1 on 13 and 492 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
plot(Reg01)

# How to looking at all the things in the output
str(Reg01)      # or you can click on environment tab in Rstudio


5. Removing variables by hand

From the Full Model, remove age

#- Backward stepwise regression
Reg02 <- lm(resp ~ . -age, data=Boston2)
summary(Reg02)

Remove indus

Reg03 <- lm(resp ~ . -age -indus, data=Boston2)

7. Exaustive Search

Go through all possible combination of variables, and find the best model using AIC, BIC, or Adjusted R-squared.

library(leaps)    # install.packages('leaps', repos='https://cran.case.edu/')

## nvmax sets max number of variables in a subset
allFits = regsubsets(resp ~ ., data=Boston2,
                       nvmax=15,
                       method = "exhaustive")

modelList = summary(allFits)
modelList

Best by min AIC

# (AIC is directly proportional to Mallow’s Cp)
ixA = which.min(modelList$cp)
print(ixA)
## [1] 11
modelList$which[ixA, ]
## (Intercept)        crim          zn       indus        chas         nox 
##        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE       FALSE        TRUE        TRUE 
##          rm         age         dis         rad         tax     ptratio 
##        TRUE       FALSE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE 
##       black       lstat 
##        TRUE        TRUE
  ### Run the best model using lm()
  ixIsItIn = modelList$which[ixA, -1]  # -1 is to remove intercept
  ixIsItIn
##    crim      zn   indus    chas     nox      rm     age     dis     rad     tax 
##    TRUE    TRUE   FALSE    TRUE    TRUE    TRUE   FALSE    TRUE    TRUE    TRUE 
## ptratio   black   lstat 
##    TRUE    TRUE    TRUE
  names(ixIsItIn)[ixIsItIn]
##  [1] "crim"    "zn"      "chas"    "nox"     "rm"      "dis"     "rad"    
##  [8] "tax"     "ptratio" "black"   "lstat"
  listOfVars = paste(names(ixIsItIn)[ixIsItIn], collapse=" + ")
  listOfVars
## [1] "crim + zn + chas + nox + rm + dis + rad + tax + ptratio + black + lstat"
  formula_string = paste("resp ~", listOfVars)
  formula_string
## [1] "resp ~ crim + zn + chas + nox + rm + dis + rad + tax + ptratio + black + lstat"
  Fit10 = lm(as.formula(formula_string), data=Boston2)
  Fit10
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = as.formula(formula_string), data = Boston2)
## 
## Coefficients:
## (Intercept)         crim           zn         chas          nox           rm  
##   36.341145    -0.108413     0.045845     2.718716   -17.376023     3.801579  
##         dis          rad          tax      ptratio        black        lstat  
##   -1.492711     0.299608    -0.011778    -0.946525     0.009291    -0.522553
  AIC(Fit10)
## [1] 3023.726
  BIC(Fit10)
## [1] 3078.671
  summary(Fit10)$adj.r.sq
## [1] 0.7348058

Best by max Adj R-sq

ixB = which.max(modelList$adjr2)
print(ixB)
## [1] 11
modelList$which[ixB, ]
## (Intercept)        crim          zn       indus        chas         nox 
##        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE       FALSE        TRUE        TRUE 
##          rm         age         dis         rad         tax     ptratio 
##        TRUE       FALSE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE 
##       black       lstat 
##        TRUE        TRUE
  ### Run the best model using lm()
  ixIsItIn = modelList$which[ixB, -1]  # -1 is to remove intercept
  listOfVars = paste(names(ixIsItIn)[ixIsItIn], collapse=" + ")
  formula_string = paste("resp ~", listOfVars)

  Fit11 = lm(as.formula(formula_string), data=Boston2)
  summary(Fit11)

Best by min BIC

ixC = which.min(modelList$bic)
print(ixC)
modelList$which[ixC, ]

In this case, AIC, BIC, and Adjusted R-squared all resulted in the same model.

  # 13 lstat    lower status of the population (percent).

## 5. Removing variables by hand

# From the full model, remove age
Reg02 <- lm(resp ~ . -age, data=Boston2)
summary(Reg02)


### Remove indus

Reg03 <- lm(resp ~ . -age -indus, data=Boston2)
summary(Reg03)



##--------------------------------------
## 6. Adding variables by hand

# Using variables that had low p-value in Chi-square test
Reg04 <- lm(resp ~  zn + indus + nox + rad, data=Boston2)
summary(Reg04)


### Remove nox from the model
# Using variables that had low p-value in Chi-square test
Reg05 <- lm(resp ~  zn + indus + rad, data=Boston2)
summary(Reg05)

plot(Reg05)


##--------------------------------------
## 7. Exaustive Search

library(leaps)    # install.packages('leaps', repos='https://cran.case.edu/')

## nvmax sets max number of variables in a subset
allFits = regsubsets(resp ~ ., data=Boston2,
                       nvmax=15,
                       method = "exhaustive")

modelList = summary(allFits)
modelList


### Best by min AIC

# (AIC is directly proportional to Mallow’s Cp)
ixA = which.min(modelList$cp)
print(ixA)
modelList$which[ixA, ]

  ### Run the best model using lm()
  ixIsItIn = modelList$which[ixA, -1]  # -1 is to remove intercept
  ixIsItIn

  names(ixIsItIn)[ixIsItIn]
  listOfVars = paste(names(ixIsItIn)[ixIsItIn], collapse=" + ")
  listOfVars

  formula_string = paste("resp ~", listOfVars)
  formula_string

  Fit10 = lm(as.formula(formula_string), data=Boston2)
  Fit10
  AIC(Fit10)
  BIC(Fit10)
  summary(Fit10)$adj.r.sq


### Best by max Adj R-sq

ixB = which.max(modelList$adjr2)
print(ixB)
modelList$which[ixB, ]

  ### Run the best model using lm()
  ixIsItIn = modelList$which[ixB, -1]  # -1 is to remove intercept
  listOfVars = paste(names(ixIsItIn)[ixIsItIn], collapse=" + ")
  formula_string = paste("resp ~", listOfVars)

  Fit11 = lm(as.formula(formula_string), data=Boston2)
  summary(Fit11)
  AIC(Fit11)
  BIC(Fit11)
  summary(Fit11)$adj.r.sq


### Best by min BIC

ixC = which.min(modelList$bic)
print(ixC)
modelList$which[ixC, ]
